--- title: Survival data and the Surv object guide-section: "Foundations" bread-crumbs: false --- ```{=html} ``` Survival analysis studies the time until an event happens: death, relapse, machine failure, customer churn, or any other well-defined endpoint. What makes this kind of data special, and what separates survival analysis from ordinary regression, is that we usually cannot observe the event time for everyone. Some subjects are still event-free when the study ends, some drop out early, and some enter late. Handling these partially observed times correctly is the entire point of the field, and it starts with how you represent the data. This page explains the structure of survival data, introduces the `Surv` object (the response type that every estimator and model in Greenwood consumes), and shows how to describe a response by column names when your data lives in a data frame. ## Why survival data is different Imagine a study that follows patients for up to two years after treatment and records the time until their disease comes back (relapse). @fig-follow-up shows four of them. ::: {#fig-follow-up} ```{=html}
``` Four patients in a two-year study. Each line is the time a patient was followed. A filled dot marks a relapse that was seen. An open circle marks the last time the patient was seen relapse-free, and the dashed arrow says the true relapse time, if there is one, lies somewhere later. On the right is what ends up in the data: one time and one status per patient. ::: Patients A and D relapsed while they were being followed, so we know exactly when: at month 8 and month 17. Patients B and C are different. B was still relapse-free when the study ended at month 24, and C moved away at month 13 and was never seen again. For both of them we only know that the relapse, if it ever happens, comes **after** the last time they were seen. Their times are **censored**: cut off before the event could be observed. So every patient contributes two pieces of information: a **time**, and a **status** that says what the time means. For A and D the time is when the event happened. For B and C it is the last moment they were known to be event-free, which is still useful information: B stayed relapse-free for at least 24 months, and that counts. Censoring is why ordinary methods break down here. Averaging the four times treats B's 24 months as if B relapsed at month 24, which makes the treatment look worse than it is. Dropping B and C throws away the fact that they did well for a long time. Survival methods use exactly what each patient tells us, no more and no less, and that is what the rest of this guide is about. ### Other ways an observation can be incomplete The example above shows **right censoring**: the event, if any, happens after the last time we saw the patient. It is by far the most common situation. @fig-kinds shows the others you may meet, and how each one is written down. ::: {#fig-kinds} ```{=html}
``` Kinds of observation, one subject per row. The shaded band is where the event could be. In **left censoring** the event had already happened by the first check. In **interval censoring** it happened between two visits. With **late entry** (also called left truncation), the subject is only observed after joining the study, so the time before entry tells us nothing about them. The right column shows the matching status code for `gw.event_time()`, and the counting-process form of `gw.Surv()` for late entry. ::: All of these are expressed through the same response object, so the estimators and models you meet later work the same way whichever kind of data you have. ::: {.callout-note} ## The key idea A survival observation carries two pieces of information: a time, and a status that says what the time means (an event, or a censoring point). You must always keep them together. Greenwood does this for you with the `Surv` object. ::: ## Ways to build a response There are two starting points, shown in @fig-ways. If your data sits in a data frame (the usual case), name the columns in a formula such as `"Surv(time, status) ~ age"`, or describe the response once with `gw.Outcome.surv()`, and pass the frame with `data=` when you fit a model. If you already hold the values (lists, arrays, or simulated data), build the response directly with `gw.Surv()`, or with `gw.event_time()` if you think in the status codes of @fig-kinds. Either way, every estimator receives the same thing: a `Surv` response. ::: {#fig-ways} ```{=html}
``` The ways to build a survival response. From a data frame, name columns in a formula or an `Outcome`. From values in hand, call `gw.Surv()` or `gw.event_time()`. All of them lead to a `Surv` response, which every estimator accepts. ::: The rest of this page walks through both starting points, beginning with `gw.Surv()` because it shows most clearly what a response contains. ## The Surv object `Surv` is the response you pass to estimators and models. It bundles the times with their status codes, so that downstream code can rely on a clean, consistent representation. You build one with a single call, `gw.Surv(time, time2, event, type=, origin=)`, which mirrors R's `survival::Surv()` argument for argument. As in R, the kind of response is inferred from the arguments you supply. The most common case is right-censored data: pass the observed times and an event indicator, where a true value (or `1`) means the event occurred and a false value (or `0`) means the observation was censored. ::: {#df8a2271 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Import the Greenwood library import greenwood as gw # Four subjects: events at 5 and 4, censored at 6 and 9 y = gw.Surv(time=[5, 6, 4, 9], event=[1, 0, 1, 0]) # Display a compact summary of the response y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` Surv(type=right, n=4, events=2) ``` ::: ::: The `repr` gives a quick summary: the censoring type, the number of observations, and how many of them were events. You can also reach the derived quantities directly. ::: {#68fa8dc0 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Read off the derived counts directly from the response print("observations:", y.n) print("events:", y.n_events) print("censored:", y.n_censored) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` observations: 4 events: 2 censored: 2 ``` ::: ::: ### The other kinds of observation Each kind of observation in @fig-kinds has its own form of `gw.Surv()`. When subjects enter the risk set after time zero, or when a covariate changes during follow-up, you use the counting-process form. Each observation is an interval `(start, stop]` with an event indicator at the stop time. This is also how left truncation (late entry) is expressed. Supplying `time2=` is all it takes: `time` becomes the start and `time2` the stop. ::: {#0f28eeef .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Each row is an interval (start, stop] with an event indicator at the stop time gw.Surv(time=[0, 2, 1], time2=[5, 6, 4], event=[1, 0, 1]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` Surv(type=counting, n=3, events=2) ``` ::: ::: The remaining types must be requested explicitly with `type=`, exactly as in R. With `type="left"`, a status of `1` is an exact event and a status of `0` means the event had already happened by the recorded time (left censoring). ::: {#baef00d9 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Status 1 is an exact event, status 0 is left-censored at the recorded time gw.Surv(time=[5, 6, 4], event=[1, 0, 1], type="left") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` Surv(type=left, n=3, events=2) ``` ::: ::: Interval censoring, where the event is known only to fall between two times, is most easily written with `type="interval2"`. The two times are the lower and upper bounds. An upper bound of `numpy.inf` (or a missing value) marks right censoring, a missing lower bound marks left censoring, and equal bounds mark an exact event. R's other form, `type="interval"`, takes the two times plus a status code (`0` right, `1` exact, `2` left, `3` interval) and is supported too. ::: {#25bc04a7 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np # The event is known only to fall in [lower, upper]; numpy.inf marks right censoring gw.Surv(time=[1, 2, 3], time2=[2, np.inf, 5], type="interval2") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` Surv(type=interval, n=3, events=2) ``` ::: ::: Competing risks and multi-state endpoints, where more than one kind of event can occur, follow R's rule as well: make the event a categorical. The first category means censoring, and the remaining categories are the states, in order. ::: {#854f374c .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd # The first category ("censor") is censoring, and the others are the states outcome = pd.Categorical( ["relapse", "death", "censor", "relapse"], categories=["censor", "relapse", "death"], ) gw.Surv(time=[5, 6, 7, 8], event=outcome) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` Surv(type=mright, n=4, events=3, states=('relapse', 'death')) ``` ::: ::: When each endpoint lives in its own time and event columns instead, `gw.first_event()` builds the same multi-state response by taking the earliest event per subject. The [competing risks](competing-risks.qmd) page shows it in action. ## Building a response from a data frame Greenwood offers two layers for building a response. `gw.Surv()`, which mirrors R's `survival::Surv()`, and `gw.event_time()` build a response from values you already hold: lists, NumPy arrays, or simulated data, as in the examples above. When your data lives in a data frame, you describe the response instead, by column names and expressions. A formula such as `"Surv(time, status == 2) ~ age"` or an outcome such as `gw.Outcome.surv(time="time", event="status == 2")` names the columns, and the estimator evaluates it against the frame you pass as `data=` when it fits. Because the description holds names rather than data frame code, it works the same on every backend (pandas, Polars, PyArrow, DuckDB, and lazy frames). That is why it is the recommended way to start from a data frame. The bundled `lung` dataset, from the North Central Cancer Treatment Group, is a good example. ::: {#bd62d34e .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Load the bundled lung dataset as a Polars DataFrame lung = gw.load_dataset("lung", backend="polars") # Preview the raw data lung ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}

So the column passes straight through, and the formula is the one you would write in R. ::: {#bdb567fc .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} # The response and the covariates in one R-style formula, evaluated against `data=` gw.CoxPH().fit("Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex", data=lung) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ``` CoxPH (Cox proportional hazards model, ties='efron') coef exp(coef) se(coef) z p age 0.01705 1.017 0.009223 1.848 0.06459 sex -0.5132 0.5986 0.1675 -3.065 0.002178 n = 228, events = 165 Likelihood ratio test = 14.12 on 2 df, p = 0.0008574 ``` ::: ::: ### Describing an outcome once When you fit several models to the same endpoint, or a model that takes no covariates, describe the response once with `gw.Outcome.surv()`. It takes the same arguments as `Surv()`, each written as it would be inside a formula, and holds no data. ::: {#171e59a8 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} # The lung endpoint, described by column names death = gw.Outcome.surv(time="time", event="status") death ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ``` Outcome.surv(time='time', event='status') ``` ::: ::: Pass it to any estimator along with `data=`. Covariates and grouping arguments such as `by=` or `strata=` can then be column names too: ::: {#db0bbd84 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} # The same description drives a Kaplan-Meier curve and a Cox model km = gw.KaplanMeier().fit(death, by="sex", data=lung) cox = gw.CoxPH().fit(death, covariates=["age", "sex", "ph.ecog"], data=lung) cox ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ``` CoxPH (Cox proportional hazards model, ties='efron') coef exp(coef) se(coef) z p age 0.01107 1.011 0.009267 1.194 0.2324 sex -0.5526 0.5754 0.1677 -3.294 0.0009861 ph.ecog 0.4637 1.59 0.1136 4.083 4.447e-05 n = 227, events = 164 (1 observation deleted due to missingness) Likelihood ratio test = 30.5 on 3 df, p = 1.083e-06 ``` ::: ::: Binding at fit time reads every column the model uses from the one frame, and it drops any row with a missing value in one of them, as R's `na.omit` does. The response and the covariates therefore can never get out of step. The printout reports how many rows were dropped, and the fitted model keeps the count in `n_dropped_`. Here, one patient has no `ph.ecog` score. A formula's response parses to the same `Outcome`, and `bind()` evaluates either one against a frame when you want the `Surv` itself. ::: {#2eb0c397 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} # The formula response and the Outcome are the same description print(gw.Outcome.from_formula(formula="Surv(time, status)") == death) # Bind the description to a frame to get a Surv death.bind(lung) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` True ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ``` Surv(type=right, n=228, events=165) ``` ::: ::: ### The expression grammar Each argument of a response is a column name or an expression. The expressions mirror what you would write in R, so a formula copied from an R script usually works unchanged. For any status coding other than `0`/`1` or `1`/`2`, write a comparison that gives a true or false value per row. The `pbc` dataset codes `status` as `0` (censored), `1` (transplant), and `2` (dead). This column must not be passed raw, because R's rules would read it as a `1`/`2` coding and mark the `0` rows as invalid. An all-cause endpoint and a death-only endpoint are each one comparison: ::: {#3572a7d0 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Load the pbc dataset, whose status has three levels (0, 1, 2) pbc = gw.load_dataset("pbc", backend="polars") # All-cause: anything other than 0 is an event print("all-cause: ", gw.Outcome.surv(time="time", event="status != 0").bind(pbc)) # Death only: transplant becomes censoring print("death-only:", gw.Outcome.surv(time="time", event="status == 2").bind(pbc)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` all-cause: Surv(type=right, n=418, events=186) death-only: Surv(type=right, n=418, events=161) ``` ::: ::: The comparisons are `==`, `!=`, `in`, and `not in`. R's `status %in% c(1, 2)` is accepted as a spelling of `status in (1, 2)`. Strings are compared the same way, which saves recoding an outcome column by hand. Missing values follow R: `==` and `!=` with a missing value give a missing status, while `in` gives false. ::: {#0c8aad20 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} import polars as pl # Build a small example with string outcomes study = pl.DataFrame({ "time": [12.0, 5.5, 20.0, 8.0], "outcome": ["died", "withdrew", "censored", "died"], }) # Only "died" is an event, and the other outcomes are censored gw.KaplanMeier().fit("Surv(time, outcome == 'died') ~ 1", data=study) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ``` KaplanMeier (Kaplan-Meier survival estimate) n events median 0.95LCL 0.95UCL 4 2 12 8 NA ``` ::: ::: For competing risks and multi-state endpoints, R's `factor(x, levels, labels)` turns a status column into a categorical. The first label means censored and the remaining labels are the states, in order. R's ranges such as `0:2` work for the levels, and repeating a label merges levels (for example, two codes that both mean censored). ::: {#8a5644e1 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} # pbc as a competing-risks response: transplant and death are separate states gw.Outcome.surv( time="time", event="factor(status, c(0, 1, 2), c('censor', 'transplant', 'death'))", ).bind(pbc) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ``` Surv(type=mright, n=418, events=186, states=('transplant', 'death')) ``` ::: ::: A time can also be computed from two date columns with `duration(start, end, unit=)`, where the unit is `"days"` (the default), `"weeks"`, `"months"`, or `"years"`. The [Data sources](data-sources.qmd) page shows it on a study export. On the right-hand side of a formula, `strata()`, `cluster()`, and `frailty()` terms route columns to the `strata=`, `cluster=`, and `frailty_cluster=` arguments. For the non-parametric estimators and the hypothesis tests, the right-hand side names the grouping column(s). ::: {#0486554e .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} # A formula for a stratified Cox model, a grouped Kaplan-Meier curve, and the log-rank test gw.CoxPH().fit("Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex + strata(inst)", data=lung) km = gw.KaplanMeier().fit("Surv(time, status) ~ sex", data=lung) gw.logrank_test("Surv(time, status) ~ sex", data=lung) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ``` TestResult(method='Log-rank test', statistic=10.3267, df=1, p_value=0.001311) ``` ::: ::: A formula's response and the arguments of an `Outcome` only ever name columns and literal values. Nothing in them is evaluated as Python code. ::: {.callout-warning} ## Check your event coding The event must be logical, `0`/`1`, or `1`/`2`. Any other value is not an error: following R, it becomes a missing status and Greenwood issues a warning ("Invalid status value, converted to NA"). Missing rows are dropped when you fit. Watch for that warning, since it usually means a column with more than two codes was used without a comparison. The section on [missing values and validation](#missing-values-and-validation) shows what happens next. ::: ### Writing it as an event-time vector Sometimes the clearest way to describe a censored time is to say what kind it is. `gw.event_time()` does exactly that. It is a port of Max Kuhn's etd R package, and it pairs each time with a one-letter status: `"e"` for an exact event, `"r"` for right-censored, `"l"` for left-censored, and `"i"` for interval-censored. For interval-censored values, `time_max=` holds the upper end of the interval. ::: {#a261b8b4 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} # One exact, one right-censored, one left-censored, and one interval-censored time x = gw.event_time( time=[7, 5, 3, 2], status=["e", "r", "l", "i"], time_max=[None, None, None, 4], ) x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ``` 7 5+ 3- [2, 4] ``` ::: ::: The printout uses the familiar notation: `5+` is right-censored, `3-` is left-censored, and `[2, 4]` is an interval. Convert to a `Surv` with `gw.as_surv()` when you need one. ::: {#c60fd1ae .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Convert the event-time vector to the equivalent Surv gw.as_surv(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=18} ``` Surv(type=interval, n=4, events=3) ``` ::: ::: You often do not need the conversion at all, because estimators accept an event-time vector directly. ::: {#65b6f7a1 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Turnbull's NPMLE fitted straight from the event-time vector gw.Turnbull().fit(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=19} ``` Turnbull (self-consistent NPMLE for interval-censored data) n atoms ambiguous iters converged 4 5 4 30 True ``` ::: ::: When the times and codes are columns of a frame, describe them by name with `gw.Outcome.event_time(time=, status=, time_max=)` or the formula response `event_time(time, status, time_max)`, just as with `Surv`. ## Missing values and validation `Surv()` follows R in how it treats questionable input. It does not reject a row outright. Instead, an invalid status code becomes a missing value with a warning, and missing times or statuses are kept in the response. The `repr` reports how many rows are missing, and every estimator drops them when it fits, as R's `na.omit` does, and reports the count. ::: {#c802f0cf .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} # The status of 3 is invalid, so the last row becomes missing y = gw.Surv(time=[5, 6, 7, 8, 9], event=[1, 0, 1, 1, 3]) # The missing row is dropped at fit time, and the printout says so gw.KaplanMeier().fit(y) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` /var/folders/s8/bj_jsx3d7jqd2btw7bwm6yx80000gp/T/ipykernel_68226/1498405665.py:2: UserWarning: Invalid status value, converted to NA y = gw.Surv(time=[5, 6, 7, 8, 9], event=[1, 0, 1, 1, 3]) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20} ``` KaplanMeier (Kaplan-Meier survival estimate) n events median 0.95LCL 0.95UCL 4 3 7 5 NA (1 observation deleted due to missingness) ``` ::: ::: The counting-process form has one more rule from R. Each start must be strictly less than its stop. A row where a subject enters and exits at the same time has no time at risk, so `Surv()` sets its start to missing with the warning "Stop time must be > start time, NA created". ::: {#1839ef47 .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Subject 1 enters at time 1 and exits at time 1 (zero follow-up), so the row becomes missing gw.Surv(time=[1, 0], time2=[1, 2], event=[1, 0]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` /var/folders/s8/bj_jsx3d7jqd2btw7bwm6yx80000gp/T/ipykernel_68226/268776079.py:2: UserWarning: Stop time must be > start time, NA created gw.Surv(time=[1, 0], time2=[1, 2], event=[1, 0]) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=21} ``` Surv(type=counting, n=2, events=1, missing=1) ``` ::: ::: If you see this warning, check your data: - **Most common fix**: exclude subjects with `start >= stop` (they have zero or negative follow-up time) - **Data quality check**: why do some subjects have identical entry and exit times? Is this a data entry error? - **If intentional**: if the event truly occurred instantaneously, add a small epsilon to the stop time: `stop = start + 1e-10` ## Serialization A response also serializes to and from JSON without loss, which is useful for saving an analysis input or moving it between systems. Calling `to_json()` returns a plain string, so you can write it to a file or send it over the wire. Here is the serialized form of the `lung` response, truncated to its first stretch so you can see the shape of it. ::: {#bf147356 .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Load data and bind the lung response to get a Surv lung = gw.load_dataset("lung", backend="polars") y = death.bind(lung) # Serialize the response to a self-contained JSON string text = y.to_json(indent=None) # Peek at the first 200 characters to see the structure text[:200] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=22} ``` '{"version": 2, "type": "right", "states": null, "columns": {"time": [306.0, 455.0, 1010.0, 210.0, 883.0, 1022.0, 310.0, 361.0, 218.0, 166.0, 170.0, 654.0, 728.0, 71.0, 567.0, 144.0, 613.0, 707.0, 61.0' ``` ::: ::: That string carries the times and status codes together, which is exactly what a `Surv` object holds. Reading it back with `from_json()` reconstructs an equivalent response, and we can confirm nothing was lost by comparing the JSON of the original and the restored object. ::: {#422ac27b .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Reconstruct an equivalent response from the JSON string restored = gw.Surv.from_json(text) # Confirm the round-trip preserved every value print("round-trips exactly:", restored.to_json() == y.to_json()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` round-trips exactly: True ``` ::: ::: For working in memory rather than as text, `to_dict()` and `from_dict()` perform the same round-trip with a plain Python dictionary, and `to_frame()` (optionally with a `format=` of `"polars"`, `"pandas"`, or `"pyarrow"`) gives a tidy, one-row-per-subject view that is convenient for inspection or export. ::: {#4f96ddae .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Export as a tidy one-row-per-subject DataFrame for inspection or export y.to_frame(format="polars") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=24} ```{=html}

This risk-set table is what Kaplan-Meier, the log-rank test, and Cox all build on, and you can compute it directly with `event_table()`. It matches R's `survfit` tabulation. ::: {#f51bd3b9 .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Tabulate events and censorings at each distinct event time gw.event_table(death, data=lung).to_frame(format="polars") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=26} ```{=html}
